en.title: Family
en.goal: Introduce family members and say how many siblings you have.

phrases.scenario: You're showing a photo and want to introduce your family. What do you say?
Someone asks if you have siblings, and you have two brothers. What do you answer?
You're telling someone your father's name, which is Marc. What do you say?
Someone asks who that girl in the photo is — she's your sister. What do you answer?

phrases.t: The father works in the city.
The brother and sister play together.
The son and daughter like school.
The husband and wife live in Paris.

dialogue.title: Talking about family
lines: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
Yes, I have a sister. And you?
I have a brother. His name is Paul.

mon-vs-ma.title: "Mon frère" or "ma sœur"?
mon-vs-ma.body: In French, the possessive agrees with the gender of the word that follows, not with the owner: mon père, mon frère (masculine), but ma mère, ma sœur (feminine) — even if you're the one speaking (man or woman). Who owns the thing doesn't matter for choosing mon/ma, only the gender of the word.

pere-mere-papa-maman.title: "Le père"/"la mère" in everyday life become "papa"/"maman"
pere-mere-papa-maman.body: To talk ABOUT fathers/mothers in general, or in a more neutral way, you use le père/la mère. But when talking directly TO your own father/mother, or about your own family day to day, the normal words are papa/maman — even among adults.

repas-dominical.title: Sunday lunch with the family
repas-dominical.body: In France, it's traditional for the family to get together for a repas dominical — Sunday lunch — which is usually longer and more elaborate than meals during the rest of the week, with several courses (starter, main dish, cheese, dessert). It's one of the times when several generations of the family come together.

review.why: 'la femme' means both; EN needs context
FR 'Voici' ('here is/this is'); EN 'This is' natural for introducing
FR 'les parents' = parents; EN 'The parents' reads oddly without context but follows the source
EN possessives (my) have no gender, so the contrast is shown through the French forms only
PT diminutive papai/mamãe has no EN equivalent; chose dad/mom (EN-GB: mum)

review.pt: o almoço de domingo em família
review.why: 'almoço' = lunch; in some regions 'Sunday dinner' is the equivalent term
